common_name: Starry Eyes Cappadocian Navelwort (Bicolor Picotee Navelwort)

planting.note: Divide established clumps in early fall or set out container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part to full shade; Starry Eyes is a sport of the species selected and named by British nurseryman John Massey for its distinctive picotee-edged flowers, and it holds a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly acidic soil in part to full shade, ideally beneath deciduous trees or shrubs where it gets bright dappled light in spring and cooler shade once the canopy fills in. Starry Eyes stands apart from the plain-blue species by its bicolor flowers, each sky-blue petal edged with a crisp white picotee margin so that a mature clump in bloom looks studded with tiny starbursts above neat mounds of hairy, heart-shaped, semi-evergreen leaves. Bloom is heaviest in early and mid spring but often continues sporadically into summer where soil stays consistently moist and cool; unlike spring-blooming Omphalodes verna, this species does not go summer-dormant and keeps attractive foliage as a groundcover through the season. Combine with hostas, epimediums, and ferns in a woodland border, and divide clumps every three to four years in early fall to keep plants vigorous.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Omphalodes cappadocica 'Starry Eyes' (AGM plant)

planting.note: Pot up divisions or rooted plantlets any time of year indoors, or set containers outside on a shaded porch or patio after last frost; Bonnie is a curly-leaved sport of variegated spider plant grown for its tightly twisted, spiraling foliage rather than the species' straight, arching leaves.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light to fairly deep shade in well-drained, moderately fertile potting mix, allowing the top inch of soil to dry between waterings. Bonnie is distinguished from the common variegated spider plant by its curled, corkscrew-twisted leaf blades that spiral rather than arch, giving a denser, more compact rosette that shows off the white-striped variegation from every angle in a hanging basket or tabletop pot. Like other spider plant selections it sends out long stolons bearing baby plantlets that can be potted up or left dangling for a cascading display, and it tolerates the dry air, fluorescent light, and irregular watering typical of indoor conditions. Repot when roots fill the container and remove any tan leaf tips caused by fluoride or excess salts in tap water by using distilled or rain water.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Chlorophytum comosum

common_name: Fire Flash Mandarin Plant (Orange Spider Plant)

planting.note: Divide offsets from the base of a mature plant or pot up nursery starts any time indoors, or move containers to a shaded patio after last frost; unlike its cascading cousin the common spider plant, Fire Flash forms an upright, non-stoloniferous rosette and produces no baby plantlets.

directions: Grow in medium to bright indirect light — it tolerates fairly low light but the petiole color is most vivid with a bit more brightness — in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix kept lightly and evenly moist, since this West African species is less drought-tolerant than the common spider plant. Fire Flash is grown for its striking broad, glossy, dark-green leaves that emerge from thick, brilliant orange-red petioles and a matching orange central leaf base, an unusual color combination among shade foliage houseplants that has made it a popular accent in mixed indoor plantings and terrariums. It stays compact and clumping, propagates readily by dividing the crown into rooted sections, and benefits from consistent warmth and humidity; cool drafts and dry air can cause leaf-tip browning. Some botanists still treat this plant under the older name Chlorophytum amaniense.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, surface-sown and left uncovered since light aids germination; plant out after last frost danger in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Confetti White is a compact, uniform F1 seed series bred for bedding and container use.

directions: Start seed indoors under lights 8-10 weeks before the last frost, pressing seed into the surface of moist starting mix without covering, then transplant into partial to full shade in humus-rich, evenly moist soil once nights stay warm. Confetti White is a compact F1 series selection bred for a dense, mounded, garden-ready habit and heavier, more uniform white speckling across the leaf surface than older open-pollinated polka dot plant strains, making it well suited to mass bedding as well as containers. Pinch young plants once or twice to encourage branching and remove the small lavender flower spikes that appear as days shorten, since flowering diverts energy from foliage and can trigger decline. Grown as a tender perennial in zones 10-12 and as a shade annual everywhere else, it pairs well with ferns, caladiums, and impatiens in a shaded bed or mixed container.
sources: Pan American Seed — Hypoestes Confetti series
